full_judgment:
9. Mr Abdul Hamid, learned Advocate for the plaintiff-petitioner submits that the trial Court on due consideration of evidence on record, decreed the suit. But the appellate Court below reversed the trial Court's judgment without proper discussion and consideration of the evidence except the evidence of DW 2. Mr. Hamid next argues that even if the plaintiff is not found in possession in respect of a part of the suitland, having been dispossessed after the filing of the suit, the present suit for declaration will not be hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act in the absence of the prayer for recovery of khas possession by amending the plaint. It is urged by the learned Advocate that the appellate Court below having held that the suit is barred by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act has committed an error of law occasioning failure of justice. 

 10. It is noticed that the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-petitioner, in course of hearing of the Rule, considered it advisable to include a prayer for recovery of khas possession of the suitland by amending the plaint and accordingly, obtained a week's adjournment. But when the hearing resumed the learned Advocate filed an application for amendment of the plaint, not for recovery of khas possession of the suitland from the defendants but for yet another declaration that the aforesaid two kabalas dated 5-4-86 executed by defendant-opposite party Nos. 3-5 in respect of the southern half of the suitland were inoperative and not binding on the plaintiff-petitioner submitting that such amendment can be made at any stage as this would not alter the character of the suit. 

 11.Mr Md Abdul Haque, learned Advocate appearing for the defendant opposite parties Nos. 1, 2, 3 and 5 contends that the preponderance of evidence on record go to show that the suit land was, in fact, purchased by defendant Nos. 1 and 2 out of their own earnings and also with the money made available by their mother by selling her ornaments and at the time of purchase defendant Nos. 1 and 2 were 18 and 12 years of age respectively and were employed in weaving factory. It is also contended by the learned Advocate that inability to file title documents including rent receipts by the plaintiff-petitioner also proves the claim of the defendant-opposite parties that the suitland was not purchased by the plaintiff-petitioner but by the defendant Nos. 1 and 2. Learned Advocate further contends that the oral evidence read with the report of the Advocate Commissioner prove that the defendant opposite parties are in possession of the suit land and the plaintiff petitioner having failed to pray for recovery of khas possession of the suitland by amending the plaint the suit is not maintainable being hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. 

 16. Since it is found on evidence including the report of Advocate Commissioner that the defendants were in possession of the suitland from before the filing of the suit, the plaintiff-petitioner was required to include the prayer for recovery of khas possession of the suit hind by amending the plaint by way of consequential relief. So, mere suit for declaration that defendant Nos. 1 and 2 are Benamders of the plaintiff-petitioner and that the plaintiff-petitioner has title in the suit land without praying for a consequential relief for recovery of khas possession from defendant Nos. 1, 4-6 the suit is liable to be dismissed being hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. If any authority is necessary in this connection cases reported in 13 DLR (SC) 228 and 39 DLR (AD) 46 may be referred to.
